ODU_108_Ọ̀bàrà_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.historical_timeline: Classical Ilé-Ifẹ̀ Antiquity (c. 9th–12th Century CE): Codified as Ọ̀bàrà-Yẹ̀kú, governing the reversal of impending fatality and the sudden dawn of wealth following hardship. Imperial Ọ̀yọ́ Period (14th–18th Century CE): Consulted by the Aláàfin's council during periods of famine and regional siege to divine royal grain reserves. Transatlantic Retention: Preserved in Lucumí and Candomblé Ketu lineages as Obara Yeku, providing remedies against premature demise and financial ruin.
ODU_108_Ọ̀bàrà_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀bàrà (I/II/II/II: royal abundance, nobility, eloquence) on the right and Ọ̀yẹ̀kú (II/II/II/II: darkness, twilight, ancestral mortality) on the left of Ọpọ́n Ifá. Dialectically balances impending tragedy with divine economic redemption, teaching that the darkest hour of despair is the herald of sovereign breakthrough when sacrifice is performed.
ODU_108_Ọ̀bàrà_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed upon Ọpọ́n Ifá with two columns: I/II/II/II on the right and II/II/II/II on the left. Involves cooling shea butter (Òrí), Ewé Òdúndún, Ewé Tètè, and a mature ram offering to Ṣàngó and the ancestors.
ODU_108_Ọ̀bàrà_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.social_and_ritual_context: Cast when a prominent leader or merchant faces simultaneous sickness, financial debt, and public ridicule. Commands urgent purification to avert grief.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀bàrà yẹ̀ ikú fún olówó; òkùnkùn kì í pa iná tí Ọlọ́run bá tàn. (Ọ̀bàrà deflected death from the wealthy initiate; darkness never extinguishes the lantern lit by the Almighty: Proclaiming divine salvation from ruin.)

Bí ìyà bá ń jẹ awo, kò gbọdọ̀ sọ fún ọ̀tá; ọ̀la ń bọ̀ tí yóò kún fún ayọ̀. (When trial afflicts the initiate, he must not lament to adversaries; tomorrow arrives brimming with triumph: Exhorting dignified endurance.)
A kì í fi owó bọ̀rọ̀kọ̀ ra ikú; ìwà tútù ni àbò ẹ̀mí. (One does not purchase death with reckless wealth; gentle character is the true shield of longevity: Warning against arrogance in prosperity.)
ODU_108_Ọ̀bàrà_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination.

ODU_109_Ọ̀bàrà_Ìwòrì.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀bàrà-Wòrì or Ọ̀bàrà-Kọ̀sọ̀, celebrating the fiery covenant between Ọ̀rúnmìlà and Ṣàngó. Imperial Era: Consulted before crowning princes of Ọ̀yọ́ to evaluate royal charisma. Diaspora Lineage: Maintained in Afro-Cuban Ocha-Ifá as Obara Koso, invoking thunderstone (Odù-Ará) protection.
ODU_109_Ọ̀bàrà_Ìwòrì.etymology_and_philosophy: Combines Ọ̀bàrà (wealth, sovereignty) with Ìwòrì (deep spiritual insight, clairvoyance). Teaches that authentic royalty must cultivate inner spiritual vision, ensuring charisma is never hijacked by sycophants.
ODU_109_Ọ̀bàrà_Ìwòrì.material_and_craftsmanship: Marked as I/II/II/II on right and II/I/I/II on left of Ọpọ́n Ifá. Prepared with Ewé Iná, Ewé Rẹ̀rẹ̀, red rooster, and palm oil poured at the base of Ṣàngó's shrine.
ODU_109_Ọ̀bàrà_Ìwòrì.social_and_ritual_context: Cast during volatile leadership disputes, unmasking hypocrites within royal courts and securing immunity from witchcraft.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀bàrà Kọ̀sọ̀ kì í bẹ̀rù àrá; ọmọ Ṣàngó kì í kú sí ilé àjèjì. (Ọ̀bàrà Kọ̀sọ̀ fears no lightning; the child of Ṣàngó never perishes in a foreign land: Celebrating cosmic protection.)
Ojú tí ó rí awo kì í fọ́; òye inú ló ń tú àwọn ọ̀tá ká. (The eye that beholds the sacred mystery never goes blind; inner discernment scatters conspirators: Emphasizing spiritual insight.)
A kì í gbé iná sórí fìlà; ọ̀rọ̀ ọlọ́gbọ́n la fi ń pa iná ìbínú. (One does not carry burning embers upon the cap; the prudent word of the sage quenches furious wrath: Teaching peaceful statesmanship.)
ODU_109_Ọ̀bàrà_Ìwòrì.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Verger, Pierre (1995). Ewé: The Use of Plants in Yoruba Society.

ODU_110_Ọ̀bàrà_Òdí.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀bàrà-Dí, the protective fortress of prosperity, guarding harvests and childbirth. Imperial Era: Invoked by market guild leaders (Ìyál'ọ́jà) to safeguard marketplace revenues. Diaspora Preservation: Preserved in Lucumí Ifá as Obara Di.
ODU_110_Ọ̀bàrà_Òdí.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀bàrà (wealth, expansion) and Òdí (protective wall, containment). Teaches that riches without institutional fortifications and moral discipline quickly evaporate.
ODU_110_Ọ̀bàrà_Òdí.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I/II/II/II on right and II/I/I/I on left on Ìyẹ̀rosùn. Uses Ewé Gbégbé, Ewé Rinrin, white pigeon, and cold cornstarch gruel (Ẹ̀kọ).
ODU_110_Ọ̀bàrà_Òdí.social_and_ritual_context: Cast when establishing new commercial enterprises or defending household estates from predatory rivals.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀bàrà dí odi yí ọrọ̀ ká; olè kì í wọ ilé tí awo fi òtítọ́ mọ. (Ọ̀bàrà erected a fortress around abundance; thieves cannot penetrate the compound built upon truth: Celebrating institutional security.)
Bí a bá lágbára láti kójọ, a gbọdọ̀ ní ọgbọ́n láti dáàbò bò ó. (If we possess the might to gather wealth, we must cultivate the wisdom to defend it: Extolling fiscal prudence.)

Ògiri tí kò l'áńfààní kì í jẹ́ kí alágẹmọ wọlé; ìwà tọ́ l'ó ń da odi sílẹ̀. (A wall without cracks denies admittance to the wall-gecko; upright character is an impregnable bastion: Teaching integrity.)
ODU_110_Ọ̀bàrà_Òdí.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Lawal, Babatunde (1996). The Gelede Spectacle.

ODU_111_Ọ̀bàrà_Ìrosùn.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Known as Ọ̀bàrà-Kosùn, celebrating royal bloodline vitality, ceremonial camwood ointment, and the cleansing of poverty. Imperial Era: Consulted during royal birth festivals. Transatlantic Retention: Revered in Afro-Cuban Ifá as Obara Koso/Obara Roso.
ODU_111_Ọ̀bàrà_Ìrosùn.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀bàrà (expansion) and Ìrosùn (ancestral bloodline, Osùn pigment). Teaches that the ancestral lineage must be washed clean of shame through honorable deeds and generous offerings.
ODU_111_Ọ̀bàrà_Ìrosùn.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I/II/II/II on right and I/I/II/II on left. Prepared with scarlet Osùn powder, Ewé Ètìpọ́nlà, rooster sacrifice, and consecrated palm wine.
ODU_111_Ọ̀bàrà_Ìrosùn.social_and_ritual_context: Cast to break hereditary poverty, heal chronic circulatory ailments, and elevate a family's societal stature.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀bàrà pa osùn kùn orí ọlá; àbùkù àtijọ́ di ẹ̀yẹ lónìí. (Ọ̀bàrà rubbed sacred camwood upon the forehead of nobility; ancestral dishonor transforms into glory today: Proclaiming lineage redemption.)
Ẹ̀jẹ̀ rere l'ó ń gbé orí ga; a kì í fi ẹ̀gbin kọ́ ilé ọba. (Noble bloodline elevates the head; one never builds the king's palace upon filth: Affirming moral purity.)

Bí osùn bá wọ awọ, a máa fi àwọ̀ dídára hàn; bẹ́ẹ̀ ni orúkọ rere ń kàn sí gbogbo ayé. (When camwood penetrates the skin, it radiates lustrous beauty; so does a righteous name echo through all the world: Praising enduring reputation.)
ODU_111_Ọ̀bàrà_Ìrosùn.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Verger, Pierre (1995). Ewé.

ODU_112_Ọ̀bàrà_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀bàrà-Wọ́nrín, governing sudden market windfalls and navigating capricious tides of fortune. Imperial Era: Consulted by caravan merchants before long-distance trade. Diaspora Retention: Maintained in Lucumí Ifá as Obara Juani.
ODU_112_Ọ̀bàrà_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.etymology_and_philosophy: Pairs Ọ̀bàrà (wealth, sovereignty) with Ọ̀wọ́nrín (whirlwind, sudden reversal). Teaches that unexpected wealth requires humility and disciplined reinvestment lest the storm disperse it.
ODU_112_Ọ̀bàrà_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I/II/II/II on right and II/II/I/I on left. Involves Ewé Àjídèwe, Ewé Ọ̀bàrà, pigeon offering, and four cowrie shells deposited at a busy crossroads.
ODU_112_Ọ̀bàrà_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.social_and_ritual_context: Cast during sudden windfalls or rapid career transitions, prescribing moderation and charity to anchor good fortune.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Afẹ́fẹ́ Ọ̀bàrà wọ́nrín kó ọrọ̀ wọlé; ẹni tó bá ní sùúrù ni yóò jẹ ẹ́ pẹ́. (The whirlwind of Ọ̀bàrà Ọ̀wọ́nrín swept wealth into the house; he who possesses patience shall enjoy it long: Exhorting fiscal discipline.)

Ọ̀rọ̀ tí a kò fojú rí kì í tú ilé olóye; ọlọ́gbọ́n ló ń ṣàkóso ìjì. (Unexpected fortune never dismantles the sage's household; the wise statesman tames the storm: Celebrating composure under windfall.)

A kì í fi owó ojijì ra ìbànújẹ́; ìrẹ̀lẹ̀ ni ìpìlẹ̀ ọrọ̀ tó ń tọ́jọ́. (One does not purchase sorrow with sudden windfall; humility is the foundation of enduring wealth: Condemning reckless ostentation.)
ODU_112_Ọ̀bàrà_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Fadipe, N.A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba.

ODU_113_Ọ̀bàrà_Ọ̀kànràn.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀bàrà-Kànràn, governing the court of conscience, integrity in commerce, and truthful speech. Imperial Ọ̀yọ́: Consulted by treasury auditors to evaluate tax collectors. Diaspora Tradition: Maintained in Cuba as Obara Kana.
ODU_113_Ọ̀bàrà_Ọ̀kànràn.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀bàrà (eloquence, majesty) and Ọ̀kànràn (uncompromising moral voice, thunderclap). Teaches that eloquence without moral truth is treacherous deception, while truthful speech yields everlasting honor.
ODU_113_Ọ̀bàrà_Ọ̀kànràn.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I/II/II/II on right and II/II/II/I on left. Prepared with Ewé Ọ́kìkà, Ewé Aragba, ram offering to Ṣàngó, and kola nuts.
ODU_113_Ọ̀bàrà_Ọ̀kànràn.social_and_ritual_context: Cast in civil disputes where perjury is suspected, commanding the parties to state the unvarnished truth under oath.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀bàrà sọ òtítọ́ kànràn lẹ́jọ́; ahọ́n tí kì í purọ́ kì í tọrọ jẹ. (Ọ̀bàrà spoke the resolute truth in judgment; the tongue that never lies never begs for sustenance: Affirming the sovereignty of honesty.)

Bí a bá ń wá ọlá, a kì í fi ẹ̀tàn gbé e ró; òtítọ́ inú ni ọ̀pá-ìtìlẹyìn ọba. (If we seek majesty, we do not erect it upon deceit; inner honesty is the king's firmest staff: Teaching ethical leadership.)

Ẹni tí ó ba purọ́ fún Ifá yóò rí ìdájọ́ Ṣàngó; àwọn Òrìṣà kórìíra ahọ́n méjì. (He who lies to the oracle shall confront the lightning judgment of Ṣàngó; the deities abhor double tongues: Demanding total transparency.)
ODU_113_Ọ̀bàrà_Ọ̀kànràn.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Barnes, Sandra T. (1997). Africa's Ogun: Old World and New.

ODU_114_Ọ̀bàrà_Ògúndá.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Known as Ọ̀bàrà-Gúndá, the divine charter of blacksmith prosperity, mechanical invention, and surgical triumph. Imperial Era: Consulted by master smiths and armorers supplying cavalry blades. Diaspora Preservation: Preserved in Lucumí as Obara Ogunda.
ODU_114_Ọ̀bàrà_Ògúndá.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀bàrà (wealth, nobility) and Ògúndá (iron, cutting force). Demonstrates that technological labor and blacksmith mastery transform raw ore into sovereign wealth and national defense.
ODU_114_Ọ̀bàrà_Ògúndá.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I/II/II/II on right and I/I/I/II on left. Prepared with Ewé Pèrègún, palm oil, roasted yam, iron slag from the forge, and a rooster to Ògún.
ODU_114_Ọ̀bàrà_Ògúndá.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for blacksmiths, engineers, surgeons, and entrepreneurs embarking on heavy manufacturing ventures.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀bàrà la ọ̀nà irin, Ògún fi ọrọ̀ kúnlé; agbára ọwọ́ awo kì í di asán. (Ọ̀bàrà cleared the iron highway, and Ògún filled the storehouse with treasure; the skilled hand of the initiate never labours in vain: Extolling industrial industry.)

Irin tí a kò kàn kì í di idà ọlá; iṣẹ́ líle la fi ń kọ́ ọ̀làjú. (Iron that is never hammered never becomes a sword of glory; diligent industry is what constructs civilization: Praising productive labor.)

A kì í fi ojú àrùn wo ọmọ alágbẹ̀dẹ; iná àrò ni ń sọ irin di wúrà. (One does not pity the son of the blacksmith; the furnace flame is what refines crude iron into gold: Teaching resilience through adversity.)
ODU_114_Ọ̀bàrà_Ògúndá.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Williams, Denis (1974). Icon and Image: A Study of Sacred Art in Five Continental Cultures.

ODU_115_Ọ̀bàrà_Ọ̀sá.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀bàrà-Sá, governing diplomatic reconciliation with mystical nocturnal matriarchs (Ìyàmi Òṣòròngà). Imperial Era: Consulted by crown envoys to defuse palace revolts. Diaspora Tradition: Retained in Cuba as Obara Sa.
ODU_115_Ọ̀bàrà_Ọ̀sá.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀bàrà (majesty, riches) and Ọ̀sá (flight, nocturnal wind, spiritual storm). Teaches that the wealthy must honor the sacred feminine forces and the elderly to preserve their legacy from nocturnal fury.
ODU_115_Ọ̀bàrà_Ọ̀sá.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I/II/II/II on right and II/I/I/I on left. Prepared with Ewé Ọ̀dúndún, Ewé Ajé, shea butter, eggs, and an offering plate placed at a junction for the Mothers.
ODU_115_Ọ̀bàrà_Ọ̀sá.social_and_ritual_context: Cast during sudden household disturbances, nocturnal nightmares, or unexplained financial attrition, prescribing propitiation of the Mothers.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀bàrà sá kúrò nínú ìbínú, ó rí àlàáfíà gbà; ìbọ̀wọ̀ fún àwọn ìyá ló ń ti ẹnu ìbànújẹ́. (Ọ̀bàrà fled from wrath and embraced serene peace; reverence for the Mothers closes the jaws of sorrow: Teaching filial respect.)

Afẹ́fẹ́ kì í jà kí ó fọ́ ọpọ́n Ifá; ọlọ́gbọ́n kì í bẹ àwọn aláṣẹ níjà. (The gale never shatters the divination tray; the prudent diplomat never provokes sovereign custodians: Admonishing peaceable conduct.)

Bí a bá lágbára, a kì í fi ba ará ìlú lẹ́rù; ìwà tútù ló ń pa iná ẹ̀sùn. (Though we wield supremacy, we do not terrorize our compatriots; gentle character extinguishes the fire of accusations: Warning against tyranny.)
ODU_115_Ọ̀bàrà_Ọ̀sá.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Drewal, H.J. (1992). Gelede: Art and Female Power among the Yoruba.

ODU_116_Ọ̀bàrà_Ìká.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Known as Ọ̀bàrà-Ká, governing the unraveling of malicious conspiracies and unmasking deceitful associates. Imperial Era: Consulted during treason trials. Diaspora Preservation: Preserved in Lucumí Ifá as Obara Ka.
ODU_116_Ọ̀bàrà_Ìká.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀bàrà (nobility, speech) and Ìká (wickedness, snare, bound cord). Teaches that integrity and divine vigilance dismantle the most insidious covert plots.
ODU_116_Ọ̀bàrà_Ìká.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I/II/II/II on right and II/I/II/II on left. Prepared with Ewé Arújẹ, Ewé Ègé, white dove, honey, and a severed cord symbolizing liberation.
ODU_116_Ọ̀bàrà_Ìká.social_and_ritual_context: Cast when an innocent person is framed by jealous business partners or family members.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀bàrà ká ọwọ́ ìkà kúrò lára ọmọ ọba; ẹni tó gbẹ́ kòtò sílẹ̀ yóò wọ̀ ọ́ fúnra rẹ̀. (Ọ̀bàrà plucked the hand of malice from the royal child; he who dug a pit shall plunge into it himself: Affirming poetic justice.)
A kì í fi ètàn mọ ilé ọlá; ọ̀pá òtítọ́ ni ń fó kòtò àdàkàdekè. (One does not build a house of honor upon intrigue; the staff of truth shatters the trap of duplicity: Extolling moral rectitude.)

Bí ọ̀tá bá kọ́ ọ̀wọ́, Ọlọ́run yóò fẹ́ wọn ká; awo olódodo kì í bẹ̀rù ẹ̀gún. (Though foes assemble in confederacy, the Almighty shall scatter them; the righteous initiate fears no hex: Proclaiming spiritual triumph.)
ODU_116_Ọ̀bàrà_Ìká.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Epega, A.A. & Neimark, P. (1995). The Sacred Ifa Oracle.

ODU_117_Ọ̀bàrà_Òtúúrúpọ̀n.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀bàrà-Túúrúpọ̀n, governing pediatric vitality, maternal blessings, and child continuity. Imperial Era: Favored by palace midwives and royal herbalists. Diaspora Lineage: Maintained in Lucumí as Obara Trupon.
ODU_117_Ọ̀bàrà_Òtúúrúpọ̀n.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀bàrà (wealth) and Òtúúrúpọ̀n (carrying children upon the back). Teaches that the true measure of wealth is the health, education, and moral stature of the children who inherit it.
ODU_117_Ọ̀bàrà_Òtúúrúpọ̀n.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I/II/II/II on right and II/II/I/II on left. Prepared with Ewé Ọ̀já-Ọmọ, Ewé Àbáwẹ̀, snail broth, shea butter, and cold maize gruel (Ẹ̀kọ).
ODU_117_Ọ̀bàrà_Òtúúrúpọ̀n.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for pregnant mothers, sick infants, and parents seeking generational blessings.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀bàrà pọ̀n ọmọ ọlá mọ́ra; ọmọ lúwàbí ni adé olówó. (Ọ̀bàrà strapped the noble infant to the back; virtuous children are the true crown of the wealthy: Celebrating generational lineage.)

Ẹrù ọmọ kì í wu ìyá lórí; pẹ̀lú ìfẹ́ la fi ń kọ́ ọmọdé ní ọ̀nà ìyè. (The burden of an infant never wearies the mother; it is with tender love that we guide the child along the path of life: Praising maternal devotion.)

Bí a bá ní ọrọ̀ tí a kò bímọ, ọrọ̀ di asán; ọmọ ni àkọsílẹ̀ tí kò lè parun. (If we amass wealth without offspring, riches become vanity; children are the living record that cannot perish: Articulating lineage continuity.)
ODU_117_Ọ̀bàrà_Òtúúrúpọ̀n.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Fadipe, N.A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba.

ODU_118_Ọ̀bàrà_Òtúá.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀bàrà-Túá, governing sacred covenants, divine intervention, and cross-cultural trade diplomacy. Imperial Era: Consulted when ratifying boundary accords with Dahomey and Nupe. Diaspora Tradition: Maintained in Cuba as Obara Tura.
ODU_118_Ọ̀bàrà_Òtúá.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀bàrà (wealth, sovereignty) and Òtúá (prayer, release, divine light). Teaches that wealth achieves cosmic sanction when dedicated to peace, philanthropy, and inter-community treaties.
ODU_118_Ọ̀bàrà_Òtúá.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I/II/II/II on right and I/II/I/I on left. Involves Ewé Ẹfun, Ewé Tètè-Àgbalagba, honey, white dove, and white chalk (Ẹfun).
ODU_118_Ọ̀bàrà_Òtúá.social_and_ritual_context: Cast during treaty ratifications, corporate mergers, and international diplomatic travels.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀bàrà tú àdúrà sílẹ̀, ọrọ̀ ń gbà wọlé; ẹni tí ó ba fẹ́ àlàáfíà kì í rí ogun. (Ọ̀bàrà poured forth sincere prayer, and abundance entered in; he who pursues peace never confronts warfare: Celebrating covenantal diplomacy.)

Àdúrà tí a fi ọkàn rere gbà ni Ọlọ́run ń kọ́kọ́ dáhùn; ìfẹ́ ará ilé ni ìmọ́lẹ̀ ayé. (The prayer offered with an upright heart is what the Creator answers first; fraternal love is the light of the cosmos: Teaching spiritual sincerity.)
A kì í fi ogun wá ọrọ̀; àdéhùn mímọ́ ló ń mú ìlú gbilẹ̀. (One does not seek wealth through reckless warfare; sacred covenants are what expand the commonwealth: Affirming peaceful commerce.)
ODU_118_Ọ̀bàrà_Òtúá.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Law, Robin (1977). The Oyo Empire c. 1600-c. 1836.

ODU_119_Ọ̀bàrà_Ìrẹtẹ̀.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀bàrà-Kẹtẹ̀ or Ọ̀bàrà-Rẹtẹ̀, governing dermatological healing, bodily purification, and victory over chronic pestilence. Imperial Era: Consulted during smallpox outbreaks. Diaspora Lineage: Maintained in Lucumí Ifá as Obara Rete.
ODU_119_Ọ̀bàrà_Ìrẹtẹ̀.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀bàrà (dignity, wealth) and Ìrẹtẹ̀ (trampling illness, bodily purification). Teaches that royal dignity requires bodily sanctity and public hygiene; physical cleanliness mirrors moral purity.
ODU_119_Ọ̀bàrà_Ìrẹtẹ̀.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I/II/II/II on right and I/I/II/I on left. Prepared with Ewé Ìrẹtẹ̀, Ewé Ṣaworo, sulfur-and-chalk bath, and cold shea butter ointment.
ODU_119_Ọ̀bàrà_Ìrẹtẹ̀.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for chronic ailments, bodily sores, or spiritual uncleanness, commanding herbal baths and dietary taboos.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀bàrà tẹ àrùn mọ́lẹ̀, ó fi ara dídára wọlé; àlàáfíà ara ni gbongbo gbogbo ọrọ̀. (Ọ̀bàrà trampled illness underfoot and entered with radiant health; sound physical vitality is the root of all wealth: Praising holistic wellness.)

Bí ara kò bá le, ọrọ̀ kò lè dùn; ìmọ́tótó ni aṣọ àwọn olóye. (If the physical body lacks vigor, wealth loses its sweetness; cleanliness is the vestment of the wise: Teaching public health and hygiene.)

A kì í fi ẹ̀gbin kùn orí àṣẹ; ẹni tó mọ́ lójú àwọn Òrìṣà kì í dọ̀tí. (One does not anoint the brow of authority with defilement; he who is clean in the sight of the deities never suffers corruption: Affirming sacred purity.)
ODU_119_Ọ̀bàrà_Ìrẹtẹ̀.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Verger, Pierre (1995). Ewé.

ODU_120_Ọ̀bàrà_Ọ̀ṣẹ́.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀bàrà-Ṣẹ́, the conduit of Ọ̀ṣun's riverine fortune, auditory honey, and artistic brilliance. Imperial Era: Consulted by court bards, royal jewelers, and musicians. Diaspora Tradition: Celebrated in Afro-Cuban Ocha-Ifá as Obara She.
ODU_120_Ọ̀bàrà_Ọ̀ṣẹ́.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀bàrà (wealth, sovereignty) and Ọ̀ṣẹ́ (sweetness, beauty, victory through joy). Teaches that harsh force repels fortune, whereas gracious beauty, honeyed speech, and artistic sweetness conquer all opposition.
ODU_120_Ọ̀bàrà_Ọ̀ṣẹ́.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I/II/II/II on right and I/II/I/II on left. Prepared with Ewé Ọ̀ṣun, pure wild honey, bronze bell (Aago), yellow cloth, and river pebbles.
ODU_120_Ọ̀bàrà_Ọ̀ṣẹ́.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for artists, musicians, traders, and women seeking matrimonial sweetness and financial breakthrough.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀bàrà bu oyin sí ahọ́n, ó fi adùn gba ilé ọba; ọ̀rọ̀ dídùn ni ń yọ ejò nínú ihò. (Ọ̀bàrà poured honey upon the tongue and claimed the palace with sweetness; pleasant speech is what coaxes the serpent from its hole: Praising the power of gracious diplomacy.)

Odò Ọ̀ṣun kì í gbẹ kí ẹja má rí ibi lúwẹ̀ẹ́; ore-ọ̀fẹ́ Ọlọ́run kì í kùnà. (The river of Ọ̀ṣun never dries up so that the fish lack room to swim; the benevolent grace of the Almighty never falters: Affirming boundless abundance.)
A kì í fi ibi san ore; ẹni tó bá fi oyin kẹ́ ayé yóò rí adùn jẹ. (One does not repay kindness with evil; he who sweetens the world with honey shall savor eternal joy: Teaching moral reciprocity.)
ODU_120_Ọ̀bàrà_Ọ̀ṣẹ́.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Badejo, Diedre L. (1996). Ọ̀ṣun Ṣèègèsí: The Elegant Deity of Wealth, Power, and Femininity.

ODU_121_Ọ̀bàrà_Òfún.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀bàrà-Fún, the apex chapter of the Ọ̀bàrà cycle, governing Obàtálá's white cloth covenant and elder wisdom. Imperial Ọ̀yọ́: Consulted when selecting the most senior noble elders. Diaspora Lineage: Maintained in Lucumí Ifá as Obara Fun.
ODU_121_Ọ̀bàrà_Òfún.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀bàrà (wealth, nobility) and Òfún (white chalk, primal purity, senior creation). Teaches that the ultimate summit of prosperity is stainless moral character (Ìwà-tútù) and reverence for the aged.
ODU_121_Ọ̀bàrà_Òfún.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I/II/II/II on right and II/I/II/I on left. Involves pure white cloth (Aṣọ Funfun), white chalk (Ẹfun), shea butter, cold spring water, and a white pigeon to Obàtálá.
ODU_121_Ọ̀bàrà_Òfún.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for high chieftains, elder statesmen, and community leaders seeking divine longevity and spotless moral reputation.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀bàrà wọ aṣọ funfun, ó fi ìwà tútù gba orí ayé; a kì í fi ẹ̀gbin kùn aṣọ Obàtálá. (Ọ̀bàrà donned the spotless white robe and conquered the world through gentle character; one never soils the sacred vestment of Obàtálá: Reverencing stainless moral integrity.)

Ọlá tí kò ní ẹ̀tàn ló ń di funfun réfeté; orúkọ rere kọjá wúrà àti fàdákà. (Nobility devoid of guile shines with brilliant whiteness; a good name is far more precious than gold and silver: Affirming transcendent virtue.)
Àgbà tí ó ní sùúrù ló ń jẹ adé ọlá; ìrẹ̀lẹ̀ ni ìyá gbogbo ìwà rere. (The elder who masters patience inherits the crown of majesty; humility is the mother of all virtues: Celebrating elder wisdom.)
ODU_121_Ọ̀bàrà_Òfún.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Lawal, Babatunde (1996). The Gelede Spectacle.

ODU_122_Ọ̀kànràn_Ogbè.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀kànràn-Sodé or Ọ̀kànràn-Ogbè, announcing the sudden dawn of truth, judicial vindication, and the banishment of conspirators. Imperial Era: Consulted before judicial trials at Akẹ̀sán market. Diaspora Preservation: Preserved in Lucumí Ifá as Okanran Sode.
ODU_122_Ọ̀kànràn_Ogbè.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀kànràn (II/II/II/I: moral conscience, thunder voice) on right and Ogbè (I/I/I/I: pristine light, opening road) on left. Dialectically represents righteous indignation illumined by cosmic light, declaring that when truth speaks without fear, all paths open.
ODU_122_Ọ̀kànràn_Ogbè.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed on Ọpọ́n Ifá as II/II/II/I on right and I/I/I/I on left. Prepared with Ewé Tètè, Ewé Gbégbé, rooster to Ṣàngó, and four fresh kola nuts.
ODU_122_Ọ̀kànràn_Ogbè.social_and_ritual_context: Cast when someone is wrongly indicted or trapped in bureaucratic deception, releasing immediate legal breakthrough.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀kànràn sọ̀rọ̀ sí gbangba, Ogbè la ojú ọ̀nà; òtítọ́ inú kì í ṣubú sílẹ̀. (Ọ̀kànràn proclaimed truth in the public square, and Ogbè opened the highway; inner righteousness never collapses: Celebrating courage and transparency.)
Bí ilẹ̀ bá mọ́, olè a gbọ́n; ìmọ́lẹ̀ òtítọ́ ló ń lé òkùnkùn ẹ̀tàn sá. (When dawn breaks, the thief scatters; the light of truth chases away the darkness of deception: Exalting triumphant clarity.)

A kì í fi ẹ̀rù bo ojú ọ̀rọ̀; ahọ́n tí kì í purọ́ ní ń gba aṣẹ lọ́wọ́ ọba. (One does not conceal the truth beneath cowardice; the tongue that never lies receives authority from the king: Inspiring fearless integrity.)
ODU_122_Ọ̀kànràn_Ogbè.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Barnes, Sandra T. (1997). Africa's Ogun: Old World and New.

ODU_123_Ọ̀kànràn_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Known as Ọ̀kànràn-Yẹ̀kú, governing the aversion of sudden accidental deaths, warding off lightning strikes, and pacifying ancestral guardians. Imperial Era: Consulted during terrifying thunderstorms. Diaspora Lineage: Retained in Lucumí as Okanran Yeku.
ODU_123_Ọ̀kànràn_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀kànràn (fire, thunder) and Ọ̀yẹ̀kú (darkness, mortality). Teaches that the fiery wrath of justice must be tempered with solemn ancestral pacification to avoid mutual destruction.
ODU_123_Ọ̀kànràn_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as II/II/II/I on right and II/II/II/II on left. Involves Ewé Òdúndún, Ewé Rinrin, black cloth, he-goat, and cold water poured over thunderstones.
ODU_123_Ọ̀kànràn_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.social_and_ritual_context: Cast to neutralize ominous portents, pacify Ṣàngó's anger, and protect households from fiery accidents.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀kànràn yẹ̀ ikú lórí awo; àrá kì í pa ẹni tí ó tẹríba fún àwọn àgbà. (Ọ̀kànràn averted death from the initiate's head; thunder never strikes down him who bows before the elders: Affirming filial reverence and protection.)
Ẹni tí ó ba gbọ́ ikilọ̀ kì í bá ogun kọjú; ìṣọ́ra ni bàbá àlàáfíà. (He who heeds sacred warnings never collides with catastrophe; vigilant foresight is the father of peace: Teaching prudent caution.)
A kì í fi iná kọ́ ilé koríko; ọ̀rọ̀ sùúrù ló ń paná ìjà. (One does not build a thatch cottage with burning flames; peaceful speech quenches the fire of conflict: Condemning reckless belligerence.)
ODU_123_Ọ̀kànràn_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Verger, Pierre (1995). Ewé.

ODU_124_Ọ̀kànràn_Ìwòrì.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀kànràn-Wòrì or Ọ̀kànràn-Adigun, governing profound diagnostic clairvoyance, unmasking charlatans, and piercing deceptive façades. Imperial Era: Consulted by military scouts. Diaspora Tradition: Maintained in Cuba as Okanran Giwori.
ODU_124_Ọ̀kànràn_Ìwòrì.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀kànràn (voice of judgment) and Ìwòrì (deep spiritual sight). Teaches that righteous judgment must always be guided by thorough forensic investigation and deep spiritual discernment.
ODU_124_Ọ̀kànràn_Ìwòrì.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as II/II/II/I on right and II/I/I/II on left. Prepared with Ewé Ìyàyà, Ewé Iná, ram offering, and clear river water used to wash the initiate's eyes.
ODU_124_Ọ̀kànràn_Ìwòrì.social_and_ritual_context: Cast when navigating complex interpersonal deception or forensic legal investigations.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀kànràn wò inú ọ̀rọ̀, ó rí gbongbo ètàn; ojú awo kì í fò lórí òtítọ́. (Ọ̀kànràn gazed into the core of the matter and identified the root of deceit; the eye of the initiate never overlooks the truth: Praising investigative acumen.)

A kì í fọwọ́ kọ́ ìbọn kí a má le ta á; ẹni tó mọ ìtàn kì í dáràn. (One does not prime the musket without knowing how to aim; he who knows the roots of history never stumbles into catastrophe: Teaching historical mastery.)

Àìwòkíyèsí ni ń mú awo ṣe àṣìṣe; ojú tútù ló ń rí ohun tí ń bẹ nínú ihò. (Inattentiveness is what causes the initiate to blunder; calm eyes perceive that which hides deep inside the cavern: Warning against haste in judgment.)
ODU_124_Ọ̀kànràn_Ìwòrì.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Drewal, H.J. & Pemberton, J. (1989). Yoruba.

ODU_125_Ọ̀kànràn_Òdí.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀kànràn-Dí, governing the protective barrier around the domestic sanctuary, immune defense, and maternal care. Imperial Era: Consulted before fortifying city gates. Diaspora Preservation: Preserved in Lucumí Ifá as Okanran Di.
ODU_125_Ọ̀kànràn_Òdí.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀kànràn (defensive vigilance) and Òdí (fortress wall). Teaches that the moral courage of a community is its most impenetrable rampart against external invasion.
ODU_125_Ọ̀kànràn_Òdí.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as II/II/II/I on right and II/I/I/I on left. Prepared with Ewé Gbégbé, fresh palm fronds (Mọ̀rìwò), iron nails, and rooster offering deposited at compound threshold.
ODU_125_Ọ̀kànràn_Òdí.social_and_ritual_context: Cast to protect families against midnight intruders, jealous neighbors, and spiritual witchcraft.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀kànràn dí ẹnu-ọ̀nà fún ibi; odi tí Ifá mọ kì í wó láé. (Ọ̀kànràn sealed the portal against malevolence; the fortress that Ifá constructs never collapses: Proclaiming impenetrable security.)

Bí ilé bá l'álàáfíà, ìta kò lè mú un; ìfọwọ́sowọ́pọ̀ ni àbò ìdílé. (If the household possesses concord, outside hostility cannot prevail; mutual cooperation is the shield of the lineage: Teaching family unity.)

A kì í fi ọ̀bẹ gé ọwọ́ ara ẹni; aládùúgbò rere kọjá ará ilé tí kò sí níbẹ̀. (One does not use the blade to sever one's own hand; a harmonious neighbor is more valuable than an absent kinsman: Praising community solidarity.)
ODU_125_Ọ̀kànràn_Òdí.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Lawal, Babatunde (1996). The Gelede Spectacle.

ODU_126_Ọ̀kànràn_Ìrosùn.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Known as Ọ̀kànràn-Rosùn, governing the healing of generational family feuds, blood oaths, and lineage reconciliation. Imperial Era: Consulted during royal succession reconciliations. Diaspora Retention: Maintained in Cuba as Okanran Roso.
ODU_126_Ọ̀kànràn_Ìrosùn.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀kànràn (voice of justice) and Ìrosùn (bloodline, ancestral camwood). Teaches that true familial honor requires forgiving ancient grievances and uniting under righteous truth.
ODU_126_Ọ̀kànràn_Ìrosùn.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as II/II/II/I on right and I/I/II/II on left. Prepared with Osùn camwood paste, Ewé Àkòko, rooster, and palm oil poured upon the ancestral stone.
ODU_126_Ọ̀kànràn_Ìrosùn.social_and_ritual_context: Cast during bitter inheritance feuds between siblings, commanding reconciliation and equitable division of estates.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀kànràn wẹ ẹ̀jẹ̀ ìjà nù pẹ̀lú osùn; ará kì í jẹ ará rẹ̀ ní yán-anyàn. (Ọ̀kànràn cleansed the blood of discord with sacred camwood; kin must never devour their own brethren: Condemning fratricidal rivalry.)
Ẹ̀jẹ̀ kì í ṣe nǹkan tí a fi ń ta tẹ́tẹ́; ìṣọ̀kan ilé ni orísun agbára. (Bloodline is not a token to gamble away; domestic unity is the fountain of fortitude: Exhorting brotherly affection.)

Bí a bá ń ja ará ilé, a kì í fún ọ̀tá l'óhùn; àṣírí ìdílé kì í já sí gbangba. (Though kinsmen dispute internally, they never betray their secrets to adversaries; the privacy of the hearth must never spill into the street: Teaching familial discretion.)
ODU_126_Ọ̀kànràn_Ìrosùn.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Fadipe, N.A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba.

ODU_127_Ọ̀kànràn_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀kànràn-Wọ́nrín, governing the whirlwind of judicial vindication, overturning false testimonies, and swift reversal of fortune. Imperial Era: Consulted by condemned prisoners seeking royal pardon. Diaspora Tradition: Maintained in Cuba as Okanran Ojuani.
ODU_127_Ọ̀kànràn_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀kànràn (thunder speech, moral indignation) and Ọ̀wọ́nrín (storm winds). Teaches that the storm of righteous public outcry quickly topples institutional injustice.
ODU_127_Ọ̀kànràn_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as II/II/II/I on right and II/II/I/I on left. Prepared with Ewé Ọlọ́jọ̀bọ́, Ewé Àjídèwe, rooster, and a small broom symbolizing sweeping away falsehood.
ODU_127_Ọ̀kànràn_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.social_and_ritual_context: Cast in contentious court battles, guaranteeing vindication for the unjustly accused.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀kànràn fẹ́ ẹ̀tàn dànù bí afẹ́fẹ́; irọ́ ní ń sáré, òtítọ́ yóò lé e bá. (Ọ̀kànràn swept away deceit like a tempest; falsehood may sprint ahead, but truth shall overtake it: Proclaiming the inevitable triumph of justice.)

Ìjì líle kì í gbé igi tí gbongbo rẹ̀ jinlẹ̀; olódodo dúró ṣinṣin nínú ìdánwò. (A ferocious storm never uproots the deeply anchored tree; the righteous statesman stands immovable under trial: Inspiring moral courage.)
A kì í fi owó bẹ ìjì kí ó má jà; iṣẹ́ rere nìkan ló ń ra ẹ̀mí lọ́wọ́ ikú. (One does not bribe the storm to cease its fury; righteous deeds alone redeem life from catastrophe: Condemning bribery.)
ODU_127_Ọ̀kànràn_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Barnes, Sandra T. (1997). Africa's Ogun.

ODU_128_Ọ̀kànràn_Ọ̀bàrà.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀kànràn-Bàrà, governing the coronation of righteous wealth, commercial rectitude, and the rewards of honest speech. Imperial Era: Consulted by guild treasurers before annual financial reckonings. Diaspora Tradition: Maintained in Cuba as Okanran Obara.
ODU_128_Ọ̀kànràn_Ọ̀bàrà.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀kànràn (truthful speech) and Ọ̀bàrà (wealth, sovereignty). Teaches that truthful dealing and moral transparency attract lasting wealth, while dishonest gains quickly ruin dynasties.
ODU_128_Ọ̀kànràn_Ọ̀bàrà.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as II/II/II/I on right and I/II/II/II on left. Prepared with Ewé Ajé, Ewé Tètè, pigeon, honey, and sixteen consecrated cowries.
ODU_128_Ọ̀kànràn_Ọ̀bàrà.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for business entrepreneurs, accountants, and public servants managing communal revenue.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀kànràn sọ òtítọ́, Ọ̀bàrà mú owó wọlé; èrè òtítọ́ kì í tán láé. (Ọ̀kànràn spoke the truth, and Ọ̀bàrà ushered riches into the house; the profit of honest dealing never runs dry: Celebrating integrity in commerce.)

Ọrọ̀ tí a fi ẹ̀tàn kó jọ kò ní gbongbo; bí afẹ́fẹ́ bá kọjá, a gbálẹ̀ mọ́ ọn. (Wealth amassed through cunning deceit possesses no deep roots; when the gale passes, it sweeps the courtyard bare: Warning against fraud.)
Ahọ́n títọ́ ló ń fa ọlá mọ́ra; olódodo kì í ṣaláìní olùrànlọ́wọ́. (An honest tongue attracts boundless nobility; the upright soul is never bereft of benefactors: Inspiring ethical stewardship.)
ODU_128_Ọ̀kànràn_Ọ̀bàrà.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Falola, Toyin (1984). The Political Economy of a Pre-colonial African State.

ODU_129_Ọ̀kànràn_Ògúndá.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Known as Ọ̀kànràn-Gúndá, the charter of righteous martial force, precision toolmaking, and defense of the defenseless. Imperial Era: Consulted before repelling bandits from trade routes. Diaspora Lineage: Maintained in Lucumí Ifá as Okanran Ogunda.
ODU_129_Ọ̀kànràn_Ògúndá.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀kànràn (righteous conscience) and Ògúndá (iron, decisive strike). Teaches that martial power is only legitimate when exercised in defense of justice and human dignity.
ODU_129_Ọ̀kànràn_Ògúndá.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as II/II/II/I on right and I/I/I/II on left. Prepared with Ewé Pèrègún, Ewé Ìná, roasted yam, palm oil, and forged iron implement to Ògún.
ODU_129_Ọ̀kànràn_Ògúndá.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for soldiers, police officers, judges, and civil defenders confronting violent threats.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ògún mú idà tọ́ ọ̀nà, Ọ̀kànràn mú aṣẹ tẹ̀lé e; irin kì í bẹ̀rù iṣẹ́ ogun. (Ògún drew the blade to clear the path, and Ọ̀kànràn accompanied it with authority; forged iron harbors no fear of martial labor: Extolling sanctified bravery.)

Ẹni tí ó mú ọ̀bẹ kì í fi dẹ́rù ba aláìlágbára; agbára tí kò ní ìrònú jẹ́ ìparun. (He who holds the dagger must never intimidate the vulnerable; power devoid of conscience is sheer destruction: Admonishing against abuse of power.)

A kì í bẹ̀rù ọ̀tá nígbà tí Ògún bá wà lẹ́yìn awo; ìṣẹ́gun wà fún ẹni tí ó dúró lórí òtítọ́. (One never dreads adversaries when Ògún stands behind the initiate; victory belongs to him who takes his stand upon truth: Inspiring valor.)
ODU_129_Ọ̀kànràn_Ògúndá.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Barnes, Sandra T. (1997). Africa's Ogun: Old World and New.

ODU_130_Ọ̀kànràn_Ọ̀sá.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀kànràn-Sá, governing diplomatic pacts between judicial authorities and the sacred Mothers (Ìyàmi), calming tempestuous rage. Imperial Era: Consulted during royal crises to avert civil wars. Diaspora Tradition: Maintained in Cuba as Okanran Sa.
ODU_130_Ọ̀kànràn_Ọ̀sá.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀kànràn (moral voice, judgment) and Ọ̀sá (flight, storm winds, female mystique). Teaches that dogmatic rigidity invites destruction; wisdom knows when to negotiate, retreat, and pacify with humble character.
ODU_130_Ọ̀kànràn_Ọ̀sá.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as II/II/II/I on right and II/I/I/I on left. Prepared with Ewé Ọ̀dúndún, Ewé Tètè-tútù, shea butter, white chalk, and cold water poured upon Ọpọ́n Ifá.
ODU_130_Ọ̀kànràn_Ọ̀sá.social_and_ritual_context: Cast to calm volatile community anger, pacify matrimonial strife, and avert female curses.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀kànràn sá fún ìjà, ó rí ìwà tútù gbà; ọ̀rọ̀ jẹ́jẹ́ ní ń fa ọgbọ́n yọ. (Ọ̀kànràn fled from pointless brawl and embraced gentle character; serene words draw forth deep wisdom: Teaching the virtues of pacification.)

A kì í fi orí kọ lu àpáta; sùúrù ló ń mú awo kọjá afẹ́fẹ́ líle. (One does not shatter one's own forehead against the granite boulder; patience is what guides the initiate past ferocious winds: Warning against headstrong recklessness.)

Bí ìbínú bá dé, awo a fòye wò ó; ẹni tó mọ̀ bí a ti ń tẹríba kì í rí ìtìjú. (When wrath descends, the initiate examines it with insight; he who knows how to bow never confronts humiliation: Praising humble diplomacy.)
ODU_130_Ọ̀kànràn_Ọ̀sá.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Drewal, H.J. (1992). Gelede: Art and Female Power among the Yoruba.

ODU_131_Ọ̀kànràn_Ìká.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀kànràn-Ká, governing the unmasking of malicious schemes, breaking spiritual cords, and triumph over malicious witchcraft. Imperial Era: Consulted during border rebellions. Diaspora Preservation: Preserved in Lucumí as Okanran Ka.
ODU_131_Ọ̀kànràn_Ìká.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀kànràn (voice of truth) and Ìká (binding cord, cunning trap). Teaches that the insidious traps of the wicked ultimately ensnare their own authors, while innocence walks free.
ODU_131_Ọ̀kànràn_Ìká.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as II/II/II/I on right and II/I/II/II on left. Prepared with Ewé Ègé, Ewé Arújẹ, white pigeon, and a severed cord signifying liberation.
ODU_131_Ọ̀kànràn_Ìká.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for individuals trapped in legal entanglements or malicious slander, securing rapid vindication.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀kànràn já àwọ̀n ìkà, ó fi òmìnira fún olódodo; ẹni tó fẹ́ pa awo yóò rí idà ara rẹ̀. (Ọ̀kànràn severed the net of wickedness and granted liberty to the upright; he who seeks to destroy the initiate shall face his own sword: Proclaiming divine deliverance.)
A kì í fi ọwọ́ mú iná jẹun; ẹni tó ń gbìmọ̀ ibi ń jẹ eérú ara rẹ̀. (One does not dine with burning embers; he who plots evil feasts upon his own ashes: Warning against malevolent conspiracy.)
Òtítọ́ ni àbò awo; kò sí okùn tí kò lè já níwájú Ọlọ́run. (Truth is the initiate's invulnerable defense; there is no cord that cannot snap before the Almighty: Affirming sacred deliverance.)
ODU_131_Ọ̀kànràn_Ìká.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Epega, A.A. & Neimark, P. (1995). The Sacred Ifa Oracle.

ODU_132_Ọ̀kànràn_Òtúúrúpọ̀n.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀kànràn-Túúrúpọ̀n, governing pediatric defense, maternal guidance, and instilling moral character in youth. Imperial Era: Consulted by lineage elders when educating young princes. Diaspora Lineage: Maintained in Lucumí as Okanran Batrupon.
ODU_132_Ọ̀kànràn_Òtúúrúpọ̀n.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀kànràn (moral discipline) and Òtúúrúpọ̀n (maternal care, carrying infants). Teaches that moral discipline must always be infused with maternal love, tempering stern guidance with protective nurturing.
ODU_132_Ọ̀kànràn_Òtúúrúpọ̀n.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as II/II/II/I on right and II/II/I/II on left. Prepared with Ewé Ọ̀já-Ọmọ, Ewé Àbáwẹ̀, cold maize pap (Ẹ̀kọ), shea butter, and snail broth.
ODU_132_Ọ̀kànràn_Òtúúrúpọ̀n.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for midwives, pediatric recovery, and families educating headstrong youths.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀kànràn pọ̀n ọmọ mọ́ra, ó kọ́ ọ ní ìwà rere; ọmọ tí a kọ́ ló ń gbé ilé baba ró. (Ọ̀kànràn strapped the child to the back and instructed him in virtuous character; the well-taught child is who upholds the ancestral home: Celebrating moral education.)

Ọ̀pá tí a fi ń lu ọmọ kì í pa á; ìfẹ́ inú ló ń tọ́ ọmọdé sí ọ̀nà ọlá. (The rod used to discipline the child never slays him; internal love is what guides the youth onto the highway of nobility: Balancing discipline with love.)
A kì í fi ọmọdé sílẹ̀ nínú ewu; àwọn ọmọ wẹẹrẹ ni ọjọ́ ọ̀la ìlú. (One does not abandon children in peril; the youth are the living future of the commonwealth: Mandating child defense.)
ODU_132_Ọ̀kànràn_Òtúúrúpọ̀n.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Fadipe, N.A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba.

basorun_oluyole_entity.title: Baṣọ̀run Ọlúyọ̀lé
basorun_oluyole_entity.description: Legendary 19th-century warlord, agrarian pioneer, and ruler of Ìbàdàn who held the imperial title of Baṣọ̀run under Aláàfin Àtìbà, turning Ìbàdàn into an imperial bastion.
basorun_oluyole_entity.historical_timeline: Classical Imperial Heritage (c. 18th century): Born into high aristocratic lineage as the maternal grandson of the illustrious Baṣọ̀run Yamba of Old Ọ̀yọ́. The Fall of Ọ̀yọ́-Ilé and Rise of Ìbàdàn (1830s): Following the devastation of Old Ọ̀yọ́, Ọlúyọ̀lé relocated to the newly established military war camp at Ìbàdàn, establishing himself as an indomitable commander through personal bravery and iron discipline. Ascension to Baṣọ̀run (c. 1836): Aláàfin Àtìbà of New Ọ̀yọ́ formally invested Ọlúyọ̀lé with the imperial title of Baṣọ̀run, restoring the ancient constitutional balance and empowering Ìbàdàn as the military defense outpost of Yorùbáland. The Battle of Òṣogbo (1840): Commanded the decisive confederated military forces that crushed the Fúlàní Sokoto caliphate cavalry expansion at Òṣogbo, forever turning the tide of the southern jihad. Agrarian & Economic Empire (1840s): Transformed military war-captives into agrarian labor guilds, pioneering large-scale yam, kola nut (obì àbàtà), and palm plantations in Ìbàdàn, establishing the city's self-sustaining economic model. Death and Immortal Legacy (1847): Died in Ìbàdàn; immortalized in ancestral oral poetry as 'Ọlọ́kùn-ẹṣin' and 'Ọba Ìbàdàn ninu oko', remembered as the chief architect of 19th-century Yorùbá military survival.
basorun_oluyole_entity.etymology_and_philosophy: The name 'Ọlúyọ̀lé' combines 'Ọlú' (Lord/Chief/Prominent Head) and 'yọ̀-ní-ilé' (rejoices in the house / brings joy to the domestic hearth). Philosophically, his leadership embodies the synthesis of martial prowess (Agbára Ogun) and agrarian economic self-sufficiency (Àgbẹ̀ Ọlọ́rọ̀). Rather than relying solely on plunder, Ọlúyọ̀lé demonstrated that enduring civil authority requires surplus food production and institutional stability, embodying the Yorùbá tenet 'Bí oúnjẹ bá kúrò nínú ìṣẹ́, ìṣẹ́ bùṣe' (Once hunger is banished from poverty, poverty is subdued).
basorun_oluyole_entity.material_and_craftsmanship: His military regalia included heavy iron chain mail, the consecrated double-edged war cleaver (Idà Ọrọ̀), and horse harnesses adorned with brass amulets fabricated by Ìbàdàn blacksmiths. In peace, he wore the flowing Ṣányán and deep indigo-dyed Kìjìpá tunics of the agrarian nobility, seated upon raised laterite daises overlooking expansive communal storehouses.
basorun_oluyole_entity.social_and_ritual_context: Presided over the Supreme Military Council of Ìbàdàn and the ancestral Ọ̀rùn festival rites in alliance with the Aláàfin. Upheld the military constitution where civilian and military chieftaincies merged into the lineage of the Olubadan.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ìbàdàn kì í bẹ́nìyàn k'ó tó jà; Ọlúyọ̀lé l'ó kọ́ wọn bí a ti ń jà fún ilẹ̀ baba. (Ìbàdàn begs no one before waging war; it was Ọlúyọ̀lé who taught them how to fight relentlessly for the ancestral motherland: Recounting martial discipline and civic pride.)

Bí oúnjẹ bá wà, ogun kò lè mú ìlú; Ọlúyọ̀lé fi àroko gbèjà Ìbàdàn. (If food is abundant, war can never conquer a citadel; Ọlúyọ̀lé fortified Ìbàdàn with agrarian labor: Celebrating economic self-sufficiency as defense.)

Ọba tí ó ní ẹṣin kò gbọdọ̀ fi ọ̀rọ̀ ọmọdé ṣeré; ìṣọ́ra ni ààbò ológun. (A sovereign commander who rides the warhorse must never trifle with vigilant intelligence; cautious foresight is the soldier's shield: Warning against complacency.)
basorun_oluyole_entity.provenance_and_citations: Johnson, Samuel (1921). The History of the Yorubas; Falola, Toyin (1984). The Political Economy of a Pre-colonial African State: Ibadan, 1830-1900; Awe, Bolanle (1964). The Rise of Ibadan as a Yoruba Power; Akintoye, S.A. (1971). Revolution and Power Politics in Yorubaland 1840-1893.
basorun_oluyole_entity.diaspora_connections: The fame of Ìbàdàn as a military fortress established under Ọlúyọ̀lé was transmitted across the transatlantic trade, referenced in Cuban Lucumí songs honoring warriors of the Oyó and Ibadan hinterlands.
basorun_oluyole_entity.media_production_notes: Costuming requires heavy hand-loomed dark Kìjìpá robes, leather talismanic bandoliers, brass-handled sabers, and laterite courtyard backdrops with large agricultural storage granaries.
